entities.summary: Marcus Valerius Volusus was a Roman consul with Publius Postumius Tubertus in 505 BC, marking a pivotal moment in the early Republic's governance. Volusus's leadership played a crucial role in shaping the Roman state's development, particularly in the areas of military strategy and diplomacy. His legacy can be seen in the subsequent growth of Rome's influence, which would eventually spread throughout the Mediterranean region. Notably, Volusus's tenure as consul occurred during a period of significant social change, as the Roman people began to assert their demands for greater representation and autonomy. As a result, Volusus's actions contributed to the evolution of the Roman Republic's institutions and the eventual rise of Rome as a dominant world power. The historian Edward Gibbon, in his seminal work 'The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire,' noted that Volusus's consulship 'marked a turning point in the history of Rome,' as it signaled the beginning of a new era of Roman expansion and influence. This era would be characterized by the Roman conquest of much of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East, leaving an indelible mark on Western civilization. Volusus's significance extends beyond his own time, as his actions and decisions had far-reaching consequences for the development of modern Western society. In this sense, Volusus's legacy serves as a reminder of the enduring power of leadership and the importance of effective governance in shaping the course of human history.

"thumbnailUrl": "", "quote": "", "legacySummary": "", "summary": "Marcus Valerius Volusus (fl. c. 500 BCE; consul 505 BCE) was a Roman Republican politician of the early Republic — one of the patrician consuls of the first generation of the Roman Republic following the expulsion of the Tarquin kings (traditional date: 509 BCE). The Valerian gens (clan) was among the most prestigious of the early Republican patriciate: the Valerians were consistently at the forefront of the early Republican aristocracy, and Marcus Valerius Volusus was one of the members of this dynasty who held the consulship in the Republic's first decades.

Marcus Valerius Volusus is recorded by ancient tradition (primarily through Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus) as consul in 505 BCE — a period when the early Roman Republic was engaged in the persistent wars against the Sabines, the Volsci, and other neighbouring Latin and Italic peoples that dominated Roman military activity in the late 6th and early 5th centuries BCE. He is also mentioned in some ancient sources in connection with the early Roman tradition of the dictator (the appointment of a single emergency commander in periods of crisis) — one of the key Republican constitutional innovations. The historical reliability of these early Republican records is contested by modern scholarship: the traditional Roman account of the early Republic was transmitted in writing centuries after the events, and the consul fasti (lists of annual magistrates) may contain interpolations and anachronisms.

The Valerian gens connection is significant beyond Marcus Valerius Volusus himself: the Valerians produced multiple consuls and generals in the early Republic, and the 'Lex Valeria' tradition (associated with Publius Valerius Publicola, the Valerians' most famous early Republican hero) — giving citizens the right of appeal (provocatio) against magistrates — was one of the foundational traditions of Roman Republican liberty.
